claim: Homeostatic regulation protects organisms against hazardous physiological changes.
source: Homeostatic regulation protects organisms against hazardous physiological changes.
evidence: This is a general statement about homeostatic regulation presented as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Homeostatic regulation is limited in certain organs and associated biological processes.
source: However, such regulation is limited in certain organs and associated biological processes.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge about the limitations of homeostatic regulation.

claim: The heart fails to self-restore its normal electrical activity once disturbed, as with sustained arrhythmias.
source: For example, the heart fails to self-restore its normal electrical activity once disturbed, as with sustained arrhythmias.
evidence: This is presented as an established fact about cardiac physiology.

claim: A biological self-restoring system can allow automatic detection and correction of abnormal excitation rhythms.
source: Here we present proof-of-concept of a biological self-restoring system that allows automatic detection and correction of such abnormal excitation rhythms.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational and experimental results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The realization of a biological self-restoring system for the heart involves the integration of ion channels with newly designed gating properties into cardiomyocytes.
source: For the heart, its realization involves the integration of ion channels with newly designed gating properties into cardiomyocytes.
evidence: This describes the approach taken in the study, supported by the computational models and experimental validation.

claim: Cardiac tissue with BioICD channels can discriminate between normal rhythm and arrhythmia based on frequency-dependent gating.
source: This allows cardiac tissue to i) discriminate between normal rhythm and arrhythmia based on frequency-dependent gating
evidence: This is demonstrated through computational simulations and dynamic clamp experiments showing frequency-dependent activation.

claim: Cardiac tissue with BioICD channels can generate an ionic current for termination of detected arrhythmia.
source: This allows cardiac tissue to i) discriminate between normal rhythm and arrhythmia based on frequency-dependent gating and ii) generate an ionic current for termination of the detected arrhythmia.
evidence: This is demonstrated through computational simulations showing current generation and arrhythmia termination.

claim: For both human atrial and ventricular arrhythmias, activation of BioICD channels leads to rapid and repeated restoration of normal excitation rhythm in silico.
source: We show in silico, that for both human atrial and ventricular arrhythmias, activation of these channels leads to rapid and repeated restoration of normal excitation rhythm.
evidence: This is supported by computational simulations shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Experimental validation of the BioICD concept is provided by injecting the designed channel current for arrhythmia termination in human atrial myocytes using dynamic clamp.
source: Experimental validation is provided by injecting the designed channel current for arrhythmia termination in human atrial myocytes using dynamic clamp.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Homeostatic regulation involves three principal mechanisms: detection, processing and effectuation.
source: Such homeostatic regulation involves three principal mechanisms: detection, processing and effectuation. The 'detector' senses a change in the environment, communicates it to a 'processor', which processes the information and commands the 'effector' to react appropriately (Horrobin, 1970).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Horrobin, 1970.

claim: Detector-effector systems are considered to be effective means to respond to changes that, if sustained, may cause harm to the organism.
source: Given their highly conserved nature, these 'detector-effector' (DE) systems are considered to be effective means to respond to changes that, if sustained, may cause harm to the organism.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about biological systems.

claim: Light sensitivity coupled to movement is an example of a detector-effector mechanism for the full scale of evolved organisms.
source: Light sensitivity coupled to movement is an example of a detector-effector mechanism for the full scale of evolved organisms, as exemplified by phototaxis in unicellular organisms (Nagel et al., 2002) and pupil reflex in higher order vertebrates (Sherman and Stark, 1957).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nagel et al., 2002 and Sherman and Stark, 1957.

claim: At the cellular level, many detector-effector systems operate through ion channels.
source: At the cellular level, many DE systems operate through ion channels, which may act as functional detector-effector units.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about cellular physiology.

claim: Ion channels can detect changes in voltage, hormones or light and respond by activation to generate a flow of ions or by inactivation to stop a flow of ions.
source: These channels can detect changes in, for example, voltage, hormones or light to which they respond by activation to generate a flow of ions (i.e. an electrical current) or by inactivation to stop a flow of ions (Catterall, 2000; Stojilkovic et al., 2010; Govorunova et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Catterall, 2000; Stojilkovic et al., 2010; Govorunova et al., 2015.

claim: A detector-effector system responding specifically to sustained hazardous heart rhythm disturbances seems not to have been evolved.
source: Although the human body maintains a multitude of DE systems that contribute to its every day function, a DE system responding specifically to sustained hazardous heart rhythm disturbances seems not to have been evolved.
evidence: This is presented as an observation about the absence of such a system in nature.

claim: Under natural cardiac electrophysiological conditions, heart rhythm disorders can terminate spontaneously, resulting in non-sustained arrhythmias.
source: Nevertheless, under natural cardiac electrophysiological conditions, heart rhythm disorders can terminate spontaneously, resulting in non-sustained arrhythmias (Bub et al., 2003; Katritsis et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bub et al., 2003; Katritsis et al., 2012.

claim: The most effective means for acute restoration of sinus rhythm in atrial and ventricular fibrillation consists of delivery of high-voltage shocks to the heart for arrhythmia termination.
source: For those that are sustained, the most effective means for acute restoration of sinus rhythm, especially in atrial and ventricular fibrillation (AF and VF), consists of delivery of high-voltage shocks to the heart for arrhythmia termination (i.e. defibrillation) (Wellens et al., 1998; Link et al., 2010; Laslett et al., 2012; Borne et al., 2013; Kumar and Schwartz, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to clinical literature.

claim: Electronic detector-effector systems have shortcomings including limited battery lives, technical malfunction and inappropriate shock deliveries.
source: Due to their non-biological nature, these electronic DE systems have a number of shortcomings including limited battery lives, technical malfunction and inappropriate shock deliveries.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about implantable cardioverter defibrillators.

claim: Major concerns from a patient's perspective are the severe pain, anxiety and depression resulting from electroshocks.
source: However, from a patient's perspective, major concerns are the severe pain, anxiety and depression resulting from the electroshocks (Sears et al., 2011), not to mention the possibility of permanent tissue damage (Ashihara and Trayanova, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sears et al., 2011 and Ashihara and Trayanova, 2005.

claim: Electroshocks can cause permanent tissue damage.
source: However, from a patient's perspective, major concerns are the severe pain, anxiety and depression resulting from the electroshocks (Sears et al., 2011), not to mention the possibility of permanent tissue damage (Ashihara and Trayanova, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ashihara and Trayanova, 2005.

claim: Three different approaches were used to design the kinetics of the BioICD channel.
source: We use computer modelling to design the kinetics of this channel via three different approaches
evidence: This is described in the manuscript with Models I, II, and III.

claim: The BioICD channel can detect and terminate tachyarrhythmias and fibrillation in both atria and ventricles once integrated into human cardiac tissue.
source: We use computer modelling to design the kinetics of this channel via three different approaches and demonstrate the possibility for human cardiac tissue to auto-detect and terminate tachyarrhythmias and fibrillation in both atria and ventricles once this type of channel has been integrated.
evidence: This is demonstrated through computational simulations shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: In simulated monolayers of human cardiomyocytes, the arrhythmia can be detected and terminated to restore sinus rhythm within seconds of its initiation.
source: We prove the concept of our study in simulated monolayers of human cardiomyocytes and in anatomically realistic in silico models of the human atrial and ventricular musculature, by showing that in each case considered, the arrhythmia can be detected and terminated to restore sinus rhythm, within seconds of its initiation, on a fully biological basis.
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: In anatomically realistic in silico models of the human atrial and ventricular musculature, the arrhythmia can be detected and terminated to restore sinus rhythm within seconds of its initiation.
source: We prove the concept of our study in simulated monolayers of human cardiomyocytes and in anatomically realistic in silico models of the human atrial and ventricular musculature, by showing that in each case considered, the arrhythmia can be detected and terminated to restore sinus rhythm, within seconds of its initiation, on a fully biological basis.
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 4.

claim: The dynamic clamp technique was exploited to realise the designed BioICD function with the use of optogenetically modified human atrial myocytes that are optically stimulated at arrhythmic frequencies.
source: In order to provide experimental evidence of the validity of the BioICD concept, we exploited the dynamic clamp technique (Wilders, 2006) to realise the designed BioICD function with the use of optogenetically modified human atrial myocytes that are optically stimulated at arrhythmic frequencies.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The BioICD ion channel should have the ability to sense the frequency of electrical activation through gating mechanisms that are controlled by the cell's membrane potential.
source: We explored the properties of this ion channel in silico and found that in order to provide the basis for a DE system, such channel should have the ability to sense the frequency of electrical activation through gating mechanisms that are controlled by the cell's membrane potential (voltage difference across the cell membrane).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling and analysis of the channel properties.

claim: Induction of a figure-of-eight reentrant source via an extrasystole during sinus rhythm results in a sustained reentrant tachyarrhythmia in a simulated monolayer without expression of the BioICD channel.
source: Figure 1A illustrates the control situation for a simulation experiment in a monolayer without expression of the BioICD channel. In this situation, induction of a figure-of-eight reentrant source, via an extrasystole during sinus rhythm, results in a sustained reentrant tachyarrhythmia.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1A showing the simulation results.

claim: In monolayers expressing the BioICD channel, the same stimulation first leads to the development of the same reentrant pattern, but then the BioICD channel is activated due to the concurrent increase in activation frequency, resulting in termination of the figure-of-eight reentry and restoration of sinus rhythm.
source: In monolayers expressing the BioICD channel (see section BioICD model I below), the exact same stimulation first leads to the development of the same reentrant pattern, however then, because of the concurrent increase in activation frequency, the BioICD channel is activated, resulting in termination of the figure-of-eight reentry and restoration of sinus rhythm (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1B showing the simulation results.

claim: The presence of the BioICD channel exerts no influence on wave propagation during sinus rhythm, both before and after the arrhythmia.
source: Of note, the presence of the BioICD channel exerts no influence on wave propagation during sinus rhythm, both before and after the arrhythmia.
evidence: This is observed in the simulation results shown in Figure 1.

claim: At any given moment in time, the number of open subunits increases with the total time spent by the cardiomyocyte in the suprathreshold (depolarized) state.
source: Thus, at any given moment in time, the number of open subunits increases with the total time spent by the cardiomyocyte in the suprathreshold (depolarized) state.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the voltage-dependent gating mechanism described.

claim: At low activation frequencies the subunits alternate between open and closed states.
source: This ensures that at low activation frequencies the subunits alternate between open and closed states (black line in Figure 2B)
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2B showing the state variable traces at 1.2 Hz.

claim: At high frequencies, temporal summation of activation leads to a higher number of subunits in the open state.
source: whereas at high frequencies, temporal summation of activation leads to a higher number of subunits in the open state (black line in Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2C showing the state variable traces at 4.2 Hz.

claim: Collective kinetics is required to render the current amplitude sensitive to changes in the activation frequency.
source: Such collective kinetics is required to render the current amplitude sensitive to changes in the activation frequency.
evidence: This is a design rationale for the BioICD channel Model I.

claim: The reversal potential of the BioICD channel was set close to 0 mV, assuming a simple pore without selectivity for any specific ion.
source: Because we require the BioICD channel to produce a depolarizing current upon activation (in line with classical defibrillation), its reversal potential was set close to 0 mV, thus assuming a simple pore without selectivity for any specific ion.
evidence: This is a design choice for the BioICD channel Model I.

claim: Channel activation occurs at high frequency, producing current only after the onset of a tachyarrhythmia.
source: As channel activation occurs at high frequency, it only produces current after the onset of a tachyarrhythmia (i.e. after a substantial and sustained increase in activation frequency).
evidence: This is a consequence of the frequency-dependent gating mechanism.

claim: Activation of the BioICD channel raises the membrane potential everywhere in the tissue to approximately 0 mV.
source: Activation of this channel raises the membrane potential everywhere in the tissue to ≈ 0 mV
evidence: This is observed in the simulation results.

claim: An additional deactivation mechanism is included to restore the initial closed state of the BioICD channel.
source: Thus, we included an additional deactivation mechanism to restore the initial closed state of the BioICD channel.
evidence: This is a design feature of the BioICD channel Model I.

claim: Abnormally fast rhythms can be detected and terminated successfully in a variety of pathological substrates in simulations of human ventricular monolayers with BioICD channels.
source: Our simulations of human ventricular monolayers with BioICD channels demonstrate that abnormally fast rhythms can be detected and terminated successfully in a variety of pathological substrates.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3 for various pathological substrates.

claim: The BioICD channel activates within 1 s after initiation of ventricular tachycardia in a substrate for VT.
source: In each case, the BioICD channel activates within 1 s after initiation of the arrhythmias, thereby electrically synchronizing the whole simulation domain within 300 ms and resetting all activity within 700 ms for VT based on functional reentry (Figure 3A and E)
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3A and E showing the simulation results for VT.

claim: The BioICD channel electrically synchronizes the whole simulation domain within 300 ms for VT based on functional reentry.
source: In each case, the BioICD channel activates within 1 s after initiation of the arrhythmias, thereby electrically synchronizing the whole simulation domain within 300 ms and resetting all activity within 700 ms for VT based on functional reentry (Figure 3A and E)
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3A and E showing the simulation results for VT.

claim: The BioICD channel resets all activity within 700 ms for VT based on functional reentry.
source: In each case, the BioICD channel activates within 1 s after initiation of the arrhythmias, thereby electrically synchronizing the whole simulation domain within 300 ms and resetting all activity within 700 ms for VT based on functional reentry (Figure 3A and E)
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3A and E showing the simulation results for VT.

claim: The BioICD channel resets all activity within 1000 ms for VF.
source: In each case, the BioICD channel activates within 1 s after initiation of the arrhythmias, thereby electrically synchronizing the whole simulation domain within 300 ms and resetting all activity within 700 ms for VT based on functional reentry (Figure 3A and E), 1000 ms for VF (Figure 3B and F)
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3B and F showing the simulation results for VF.

claim: The BioICD channel resets all activity within 1000 ms for VT in fibrosis.
source: In each case, the BioICD channel activates within 1 s after initiation of the arrhythmias, thereby electrically synchronizing the whole simulation domain within 300 ms and resetting all activity within 700 ms for VT based on functional reentry (Figure 3A and E), 1000 ms for VF (Figure 3B and F) and VT in fibrosis (Figure 3C and G)
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3C and G showing the simulation results for VT in fibrosis.

claim: The BioICD channel resets all activity within 600 ms for anatomical reentry.
source: In each case, the BioICD channel activates within 1 s after initiation of the arrhythmias, thereby electrically synchronizing the whole simulation domain within 300 ms and resetting all activity within 700 ms for VT based on functional reentry (Figure 3A and E), 1000 ms for VF (Figure 3B and F) and VT in fibrosis (Figure 3C and G), and 600 ms for anatomical reentry (Figure 3D and H).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3D and H showing the simulation results for anatomical reentry.

claim: Sinus rhythm resumes in all cases once the electrophysiological steady state has been restored.
source: Sinus rhythm resumes in all cases, once the electrophysiological steady state has been restored.
evidence: This is observed in the simulation results shown in Figure 3.

claim: The entire process from arrhythmia initiation to restoration of sinus rhythm takes about 2 s in the ventricular monolayers.
source: Thus, the entire process from arrhythmia initiation to restoration of sinus rhythm takes about 2 s in the ventricular monolayers.
evidence: This is based on the timing data from the simulations shown in Figure 3.

claim: In substrates with more fibrosis (30% instead of 20% fibroblasts), the BioICD model is still able to auto-detect and terminate VT albeit somewhat slower.
source: In substrates with more fibrosis (30% instead of 20% fibroblasts as in Figure 3C and G), our BioICD model is still able to auto-detect and terminate VT albeit somewhat slower (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated based on additional simulations not shown in the figures.

claim: The presence of the BioICD channel exerts no significant influence on the AP at sinus rhythm (1.2 Hz).
source: As shown in Figure 3I, the presence of the BioICD channel exerts no significant influence on the AP at sinus rhythm (1.2 Hz) (the black and orange traces coincide)
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3I showing overlapping AP traces at 1.2 Hz.

claim: The BioICD channel slightly increases the APD at close-to-arrhythmic frequencies.
source: As shown in Figure 3I, the presence of the BioICD channel exerts no significant influence on the AP at sinus rhythm (1.2 Hz) (the black and orange traces coincide), but slightly increases the APD at close-to-arrhythmic frequencies.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3I showing AP traces at higher frequencies.

claim: The BioICD channel effectively increases the minimal APD of the cardiomyocytes.
source: This is also accounted for in the APD restitution curve of Figure 3J, which shows that the BioICD channel effectively increases the minimal APD of the cardiomyocytes.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3J showing the APD restitution curve.

claim: The BioICD channels are unable to detect and eliminate reentrant activity anchored to scars if the activation frequency is too low.
source: As a consequence of their sensitivity to frequency, the BioICD channels are unable to detect and eliminate reentrant activity anchored to scars if the activation frequency is too low, for example in substrates with large scars (see Video 5 in the Supporting Information).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Video 5 showing failure of termination with a large scar.

claim: The BioICD channel successfully detects and terminates sustained fibrillation in both ventricles and atria to restore sinus rhythm in anatomically realistic human hearts.
source: Next, we incorporated the BioICD channel in cardiomyocytes of anatomically realistic human atria and ventricles. We find that the same channel successfully detects and terminates sustained fibrillation in both ventricles and atria to restore sinus rhythm, as illustrated in Figure 4A and B
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4A and B showing the simulation results in anatomically realistic models.

claim: The mechanism of defibrillation in anatomically realistic hearts is similar to that in monolayers.
source: The mechanism of defibrillation is similar to that in monolayers.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the simulation results in monolayers and anatomically realistic models.

claim: Arrhythmia-triggered activation of the BioICD channel in some regions leads to complete reset of the cells, whereas in others it prolongs APD, leading to extinction of the arrhythmia sources.
source: Arrhythmia-triggered activation of the BioICD channel in some regions leads to complete reset of the cells, whereas in others it prolongs APD, leading to extinction of the arrhythmia sources.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of arrhythmia termination observed in the simulations.

claim: The BioICD channels in human atria could detect ongoing AF within 1.7 s.
source: With our choice of parameters, the BioICD channels in human atria could detect ongoing AF within 1.7 s and terminate it within 1.2 s to restore sinus rhythm.
evidence: This is based on the timing data from the simulations in anatomically realistic atria.

claim: The BioICD channels in human atria could terminate AF within 1.2 s to restore sinus rhythm.
source: With our choice of parameters, the BioICD channels in human atria could detect ongoing AF within 1.7 s and terminate it within 1.2 s to restore sinus rhythm.
evidence: This is based on the timing data from the simulations in anatomically realistic atria.

claim: The BioICD channels in the ventricles could detect VF within 3 s.
source: The corresponding channels in the ventricles could detect VF within 3 s and terminate it within 500 ms to restore sinus rhythm.
evidence: This is based on the timing data from the simulations in anatomically realistic ventricles.

claim: The BioICD channels in the ventricles could terminate VF within 500 ms to restore sinus rhythm.
source: The corresponding channels in the ventricles could detect VF within 3 s and terminate it within 500 ms to restore sinus rhythm.
evidence: This is based on the timing data from the simulations in anatomically realistic ventricles.

claim: The BioICD current was mimicked in vitro using dynamic patch-clamping.
source: In order to assess, in actual cardiomyocytes, the anti-arrhythmic effect of the BioICD channel, the BioICD current was mimicked in vitro using dynamic patch-clamping (Wilders, 2006).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used for validation.

claim: Dynamic patch-clamping can be used to introduce virtual voltage-gated ion channels into electrically excitable cells such as cardiomyocytes.
source: This technique can be used to introduce virtual voltage-gated ion channels (like the BioICD channel) into electrically excitable cells such as cardiomyocytes, in this case human atrial myocytes derived from a conditionally immortalized cell line (Harlaar et al., 2019; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wilders, 2006 and demonstrated in the experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Human atrial myocytes were optogenetically modified to control their excitation rhythm by light using a dynamically controlled LED source.
source: These cells were optogenetically modified (Feola et al., 2016; Figure 5E) to control their excitation rhythm by light using a dynamically controlled LED source.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Feola et al., 2016 and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The dynamic clamp experiment was carried out in current clamp mode, which allowed the unbiased recording of the membrane potential.
source: The dynamic clamp experiment was carried out in current clamp mode, which allowed the unbiased recording of the membrane potential as it develops as the net result of the activity of all endogenous ion channels and the BioICD channel.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used.

claim: The real-time measured membrane potential was used to calculate the amplitude of the BioICD current, which was injected into the cell via the recording electrode.
source: The real-time measured membrane potential was used to calculate the amplitude of the BioICD current, which was injected into the cell via the recording electrode.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used.

claim: A real-time interface between the patch-clamp amplifier and a computer constituted the feedback loop that allowed mimicking the presence of the BioICD channel.
source: A real-time interface between the patch-clamp amplifier and a computer constituted the feedback loop (Figure 5B) that allowed us to mimic the presence of the BioICD channel, and to observe the effects of BioICD channel activity in cardiomyocytes (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The same ion channel gating properties used for the in silico studies successfully detected fast pacing rhythms in a living cell.
source: We found that the same ion channel gating properties used for the in silico studies successfully detected fast pacing rhythms in a living cell.
evidence: This is based on the experimental results shown in Figure 5.

claim: No significant distortions of AP were registered at 1 Hz.
source: While no significant distortions of AP were registered at 1 Hz (the black and orange traces coincide), the depolarizing current produced by the BioICD channel at high frequencies built up resulting in APD prolongation.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the experimental traces shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: The depolarizing current produced by the BioICD channel at high frequencies built up resulting in APD prolongation.
source: While no significant distortions of AP were registered at 1 Hz (the black and orange traces coincide), the depolarizing current produced by the BioICD channel at high frequencies built up resulting in APD prolongation.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the experimental traces shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: The process of arrhythmia detection, current accumulation, and pacing block is frequency-dependent.
source: This process of arrhythmia detection, current accumulation, and pacing block is frequency-dependent, as evidenced by the smaller time until termination following 8 Hz optical pacing (1.16 s, Figure 5D) versus 7 Hz pacing (1.92 s, Figure 5C) within the same cell.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the experimental results at different frequencies shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: The frequency at which termination occurs is dependent on the baseline APD.
source: The frequency at which termination occurs is also dependent on the baseline APD (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5G showing the relationship between baseline APD and maximal BCL for termination.

claim: Upon an increase in baseline APD, the BioICD channel is activated earlier, namely at longer BCLs.
source: Upon an increase in baseline APD, the BioICD channel is activated earlier, namely at longer BCLs.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5G showing the relationship between baseline APD and maximal BCL for termination.

claim: The proposed ionic gating mechanism is able to restore cardiac excitation rhythm in living excitable cells.
source: Collectively, these findings show that the proposed ionic gating mechanism is able to restore cardiac excitation rhythm in living excitable cells.
evidence: This is based on the experimental results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Arrhythmia detection relies on positive feedback upon frequency increase.
source: Here, arrhythmia detection relies on positive feedback upon frequency increase.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of the BioICD channel.

claim: Three possible realisations of anti-arrhythmic gating are described in the different BioICD models I-III.
source: We propose three possible realisations of such anti-arrhythmic gating, as described in the different BioICD models I-III.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the models presented in the manuscript.

claim: The BioICD models should not be viewed as the ultimate designs of a BioICD channel, but more as a first set of rigorous outlines that can serve as a basis for additional research.
source: However, these should not be viewed as the ultimate designs of a BioICD channel, but more as a first set of rigorous outlines that can serve as a basis for additional research now that the concept has been proven in the virtual human heart.
evidence: This is a statement about the scope and limitations of the current work.

claim: Changing time constants will alter the activation time course of the channel, which can result in a shorter or longer delay preceding arrhythmia termination.
source: Also, changing time constants will alter the activation time course of the channel, which can result in a shorter or longer delay preceding arrhythmia termination.
evidence: This is a statement about potential modifications to the model.

claim: The structure of the BioICD model allows ample freedom to choose kinetic as well as threshold parameters for the channel within certain limits.
source: Indeed, the structure of our BioICD model allows ample freedom to choose kinetic as well as threshold parameters for the channel within certain limits.
evidence: This is a statement about the flexibility of the model design.

claim: The BioICD channels were tested in homogeneous, anatomically realistic atria and ventricles as proof-of-principle in the virtual human heart.
source: As proof-of-principle in the virtual human heart, we tested the BioICD channels in homogeneous, anatomically realistic atria and ventricles.
evidence: This describes the scope of the computational studies.

claim: The model should also work for pathological substrates where the arrhythmia comes with an increase in activation frequency.
source: Based on our dynamic patch-clamp experiments, we conjecture that the model should also work for pathological substrates where the arrhythmia comes with an increase in activation frequency.
evidence: This is a conjecture based on the experimental results.

claim: The mechanism for self-restoration of cardiac excitation rhythm relies only on the detection of high-frequency signals, irrespective of the nature and underlying cause of the arrhythmia.
source: This is based on the notion that the mechanism for self-restoration of cardiac excitation rhythm relies only on the detection of high-frequency signals, irrespective of the nature and underlying cause of the arrhythmia.
evidence: This is a statement about the generality of the mechanism.

claim: Not all high-frequency arrhythmias are sustained in nature.
source: Note that, in nature, not all high-frequency arrhythmias are sustained.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about cardiac arrhythmias.

claim: A significant fraction of high-frequency arrhythmias does get self-terminated.
source: A significant fraction does get self-terminated (Josephson and Kastor, 1977)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Josephson and Kastor, 1977.

claim: The mechanisms behind spontaneous termination of arrhythmias are still up for speculation.
source: although the mechanisms behind such spontaneous termination are still up for speculation.
evidence: This is presented as a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Reentrant circuits can act as feedback systems in which changes in the duration of one cycle have the potential to affect conduction in the subsequent cycles.
source: For example, reentrant circuits can act as feedback systems in which changes in the duration of one cycle have the potential to affect conduction in the subsequent cycles (Frame and Rhee, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Frame and Rhee, 1991.

claim: Cycle length was found to oscillate with progressively increasing alternations of long and short periods until a sufficiently short cycle led to conduction block.
source: Cycle length was found to oscillate with progressively increasing alternations of long and short periods until a sufficiently short cycle led to conduction block (Ortiz et al., 1993; Frame and Simson, 1988; Quan and Rudy, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ortiz et al., 1993; Frame and Simson, 1988; Quan and Rudy, 1990.

claim: A feedback system with cycle length oscillations was studied in silico and in vivo in the atrioventricular-node.
source: A feedback system with the aforementioned characteristic was studied in silico and in vivo in the atrioventricular-node (Simson et al., 1981; Sun et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Simson et al., 1981; Sun et al., 1995.

claim: A frequency-based feedback system exists in the atrioventricular and sinoatrial nodes in the heart, where overdrive suppression creates block of nodal activation.
source: Also, a frequency-based feedback system exists in the atrioventricular and sinoatrial nodes in the heart, where overdrive suppression creates block of nodal activation (Kunysz et al., 1995; Vassalle, 1970; Kunysz et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kunysz et al., 1995; Vassalle, 1970; Kunysz et al., 1997.

claim: Nagai et al., 2000 demonstrated a way to end paroxysmal arrhythmias based on overdrive suppression in a circular ring of regular cardiac cells interspersed with two pacemakers.
source: In addition, Nagai et al., 2000 demonstrated a way to end paroxysmal arrhythmias based on overdrive suppression in a circular ring of regular cardiac cells interspersed with two pacemakers.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nagai et al., 2000.

claim: Unstable tachycardias demonstrate cycle length oscillations that can lead to spontaneous termination of the tachycardia.
source: Interestingly, whereas unstable tachycardias demonstrate cycle length oscillations that can lead to spontaneous termination of the tachycardia, stable tachycardias exhibit damped oscillations when perturbed.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about tachycardia dynamics.

claim: Stable tachycardias exhibit damped oscillations when perturbed.
source: Interestingly, whereas unstable tachycardias demonstrate cycle length oscillations that can lead to spontaneous termination of the tachycardia, stable tachycardias exhibit damped oscillations when perturbed.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about tachycardia dynamics.

claim: Damped oscillations in stable tachycardias can still lead to sustained reentry.
source: Despite the phenomena discussed above, these damped oscillations can still lead to sustained reentry.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about tachycardia dynamics.

claim: The study focused on developing a detector-effector system capable of handling sustained arrhythmias, including the most hazardous ones like fibrillation.
source: In the present study, we focused on developing a DE system capable of handling sustained arrhythmias, including the most hazardous ones like fibrillation.
evidence: This describes the focus and scope of the study.

claim: The BioICD model allows for the detection and elimination of relatively fast sustained rhythms, thereby targeting those arrhythmias that require intervention for acute termination.
source: As a consequence of the design, this particular BioICD model allows for the detection and elimination of relatively fast sustained rhythms, thereby targeting those arrhythmias that require intervention for acute termination.
evidence: This is a consequence of the design choices made for the BioICD channel.

claim: Relatively low frequency arrhythmias are not detected by the BioICD channel and are therefore also not terminated.
source: This means that relatively low frequency arrhythmias are not detected by the BioICD channel and are therefore also not terminated.
evidence: This is a consequence of the frequency-dependent detection mechanism.

claim: A reentrant wave anchored to an anatomical obstacle with a large perimeter is an example of a low frequency arrhythmia not detected by the BioICD channel.
source: An example is a reentrant wave anchored to an anatomical obstacle (i.e. a scar) with a large perimeter (see Supporting Information, Video 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Video 5 showing failure of detection and termination.

claim: Low-frequency arrhythmias are considered to be less hazardous than those with a high frequency, like fibrillation.
source: However, as low-frequency arrhythmias are considered to be less hazardous than those with a high frequency, like fibrillation, they can be managed otherwise (Cho and Marbán, 2010; Stevenson, 2013; Nattel et al., 2014; Bongianino and Priori, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: All the essential knowledge about ion channel structure-function relationships is available for the construction of a BioICD channel.
source: We believe that, for the construction of a BioICD channel, all the essential knowledge about ion channel structure-function relationships (Börjesson and Elinder, 2008; Catterall, 2010; Moreau et al., 2014), as well as the molecular tools to manipulate these relationships in a systemic and rational manner are available (Bayley and Jayasinghe, 2004; Subramanyam and Colecraft, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on ion channel structure-function relationships and molecular tools.

claim: The molecular tools to manipulate ion channel structure-function relationships in a systemic and rational manner are available.
source: We believe that, for the construction of a BioICD channel, all the essential knowledge about ion channel structure-function relationships (Börjesson and Elinder, 2008; Catterall, 2010; Moreau et al., 2014), as well as the molecular tools to manipulate these relationships in a systemic and rational manner are available (Bayley and Jayasinghe, 2004; Subramanyam and Colecraft, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on molecular tools.

claim: Ion channels from which functions can serve as a blueprint are not limited to eukaryotic organisms only, but encompass prokaryotic ones as well.
source: The ion channels from which functions can serve as a blueprint are not limited to eukaryotic organisms only, but encompass prokaryotic ones as well (Ren et al., 2001; Martinac et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ren et al., 2001; Martinac et al., 2008.

claim: Ion channels can be searched for in extensive databases, such as the IUPHAR/BPS.
source: and can be searched for in extensive databases, such as the IUPHAR/BPS (Southan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Southan et al., 2016.

claim: The field of optogenetics has allowed the study of biological arrhythmia termination and could thereby add to the translation of the findings.
source: Also, the field of optogenetics has allowed the study of biological arrhythmia termination and could thereby add to the translation of our findings (Boyle et al., 2018; Entcheva and Bub, 2016; Boyden et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to optogenetics literature.

claim: Cardiomyocytes are able to generate sufficient electrical current, based on the natural electrochemical gradients, for biological auto-termination of both atrial and ventricular arrhythmias, including fibrillation.
source: In earlier work from our group and others, it was shown that cardiomyocytes are indeed able to generate sufficient electrical current, based on the natural electrochemical gradients, for biological auto-termination of both atrial and ventricular arrhythmias, including fibrillation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Biological auto-termination of arrhythmias was shown in vitro using monolayers of neonatal atrial myocytes.
source: This was shown in vitro using monolayers of neonatal atrial myocytes (Bingen et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bingen et al., 2014.

claim: Biological auto-termination of arrhythmias was shown in the whole heart of adult rodents.
source: but later also in the whole heart of adult rodents (Bruegmann et al., 2016; Crocini et al., 2016; Nyns et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bruegmann et al., 2016; Crocini et al., 2016; Nyns et al., 2016.

claim: Biological auto-termination of arrhythmias was integrated in a hybrid bio-electronic system.
source: and most recently also integrated in a hybrid bio-electronic system (Nyns et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nyns et al., 2019.

claim: In previous studies, the gating of ion channels was controlled by light to terminate cardiac arrhythmias.
source: In these studies, the gating of ion channels was controlled by light to terminate cardiac arrhythmias.
evidence: This describes previous work in the field.

claim: The study shows how ion channel gating could be controlled by the arrhythmia itself, thereby giving rise to a new fully biological detector-effector system.
source: As a next step, we now show how such gating could be controlled by the arrhythmia itself, thereby giving rise to a new fully biological DE system.
evidence: This describes the novel contribution of the current study.

claim: Optogenetics was used to provide experimental proof of the BioICD concept with the use of human atrial myocytes.
source: In this study, we used optogenetics to provide experimental proof of the aforementioned concept with the use of human atrial myocytes.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used for validation.

claim: Atrial myocytes were optogenetically modified and used in dynamic patch-clamp experiments to separate the pacing mechanism (optical) from the rhythm restoration mechanism (chemical/electrical) in order to improve signal interpretation.
source: These atrial myocytes were optogenetically modified and used in dynamic patch-clamp experiments to separate the pacing mechanism (optical) from the rhythm restoration mechanism (chemical/electrical) in order to improve signal interpretation, that is stimulation block at depolarised membrane potentials.
evidence: This describes the rationale for the experimental design.

claim: The in vitro data show the same phenomenological phases as visible in the traces coming from the in silico simulations.
source: Our studies reveal that the in vitro data (Figure 5C–D) show the same phenomenological phases as visible in the traces coming from the in silico simulations (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental and simulation results shown in Figures 1 and 5.

claim: The BioICD channel is capable of restoring normal excitation rhythm in cells with short baseline APDs under high frequency.
source: Because the BioICD channel is capable of restoring normal excitation rhythm in cells with short baseline APDs under high frequency, the design of the gating properties makes that such restoration will work also for cells with long baseline APDs (Figures 2 and 5G), like those found in ventricular myocytes.
evidence: This is based on the experimental results shown in Figures 2 and 5G.

claim: The design of the gating properties makes that restoration will work also for cells with long baseline APDs, like those found in ventricular myocytes.
source: Because the BioICD channel is capable of restoring normal excitation rhythm in cells with short baseline APDs under high frequency, the design of the gating properties makes that such restoration will work also for cells with long baseline APDs (Figures 2 and 5G), like those found in ventricular myocytes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results and the design of the BioICD channel.

claim: The decision to use an atrial cell line for the experimental validation was motivated by the fact that the BioICD channel is capable of restoring normal excitation rhythm in cells with short baseline APDs.
source: This motivated our decision to use an atrial cell line for the experimental validation of our proposed concept.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the experimental design choice.

claim: The study presents insight into acquired homeostatic regulation of excitation rhythm under disturbed conditions, including cardiac fibrillation.
source: Taken together, our study presents insight into acquired homeostatic regulation of excitation rhythm under disturbed conditions, including cardiac fibrillation.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the contribution of the study.

claim: Homeostatic regulation of excitation rhythm can be established by creation of a biologically engineered detector-effector system for arrhythmias through expression of customized ion channels.
source: It is shown, by a combination of theoretical and experimental studies, that such regulation can be established by creation of a biologically engineered DE system for arrhythmias through expression of customized ion channels.
evidence: This is supported by the computational and experimental results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Self-resetting of an acutely disturbed heart rhythm by an engineered biological detector-effector system may yield unique insight into arrhythmia management.
source: Self-resetting of an acutely disturbed heart rhythm by an engineered biological DE system may yield unique insight into arrhythmia management
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential impact of the work.

claim: Self-resetting of an acutely disturbed heart rhythm may lay the foundation for the development of distinctively innovative treatment options by the creation of new biology for therapeutic purposes.
source: Self-resetting of an acutely disturbed heart rhythm by an engineered biological DE system may yield unique insight into arrhythmia management and may lay the foundation for the development of distinctively innovative treatment options by the creation of new biology for therapeutic purposes, ultimately leading to acute, yet trauma-free termination of arrhythmias.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential impact of the work.

claim: The approach could ultimately lead to acute, yet trauma-free termination of arrhythmias.
source: Self-resetting of an acutely disturbed heart rhythm by an engineered biological DE system may yield unique insight into arrhythmia management and may lay the foundation for the development of distinctively innovative treatment options by the creation of new biology for therapeutic purposes, ultimately leading to acute, yet trauma-free termination of arrhythmias.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential clinical application.

claim: This approach would stretch the field of synthetic biology into cardiology.
source: This would stretch the field of synthetic biology into cardiology and also provide a radically new perspective for other medical fields, given the general nature and versatility of biological DE systems.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader impact of the work.

claim: This approach would provide a radically new perspective for other medical fields, given the general nature and versatility of biological detector-effector systems.
source: This would stretch the field of synthetic biology into cardiology and also provide a radically new perspective for other medical fields, given the general nature and versatility of biological DE systems.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader impact of the work.

claim: The perspective involves that a diseased organ begets its own remedy, for example a Biologically Integrated Cardiac Defibrillator (BioICD) in case of the heart.
source: This perspective involves that a diseased organ, begets its own remedy, for example a Biologically Integrated Cardiac Defibrillator (BioICD) in case of the heart.
evidence: This is a conceptual statement about the philosophy behind the approach.

claim: The mathematical model proposed by Ten Tusscher et al., 2009 was used for human ventricular tissue.
source: For human ventricular tissue, the mathematical model proposed by Ten Tusscher et al., 2009 was used
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ten Tusscher et al., 2009.

claim: The model for fibrosis contained 20% randomly distributed fibroblasts, which did not couple electrotonically to the neighbouring cardiomyocytes.
source: Our model for fibrosis contained 20% randomly distributed fibroblasts, which did not couple electrotonically to the neighbouring cardiomyocytes (Ten Tusscher and Panfilov, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ten Tusscher and Panfilov, 2007.

claim: For human atrial tissue, data and fibre directions were obtained from Dössel et al., 2011.
source: For human atrial tissue, data and fibre directions were obtained from Dössel et al., 2011.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dössel et al., 2011.

claim: The ionic cell model used for human atrial tissue is the AF-induced electrically remodelled human atrial Courtemanche et al., 1999 model.
source: The ionic cell model that was used is the AF-induced electrically remodelled human atrial Courtemanche et al., 1999 model (adapted from Courtemanche et al., 1998, which was taken from CellML (Yu et al., 2011) with the use of Myokit (Clerx et al., 2016) and transformed to graphics processing unit-usable code).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Courtemanche et al., 1999, Courtemanche et al., 1998, Yu et al., 2011, and Clerx et al., 2016.

claim: An S1-S2 cross-field protocol was used to generate spiral and scroll waves.
source: We used an S1-S2 cross-field protocol to generate spiral and scroll waves (ten Tusscher and Panfilov, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to ten Tusscher and Panfilov, 2006.

claim: The cell line used was generated by transducing human foetal atrial myocytes with a human immunodeficiency virus type 1-based vector conferring doxycycline-controlled expression of simian virus 40 large tumour antigen.
source: The cell line used in this study has recently been generated by transducing human foetal atrial myocytes with a human immunodeficiency virus type 1-based vector conferring doxycycline-controlled expression of simian virus 40 large tumour antigen as described in Harlaar et al., 2019.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Harlaar et al., 2019.

claim: The cells were tested negative for the presence of mycoplasma.
source: The cells were tested negative for the presence of mycoplasma by the MycoAlert mycoplasma detection kit (Lonza, Basel, Switzerland), as well as by Hoechst 33342 (Life Technologies Europe, Bleiswijk, the Netherlands) staining of Vero cells cultured with conditioned human atrial myocyte medium.
evidence: This describes the quality control procedures for the cell line.

claim: Self-inactivating lentiviral vector particles encoding an eYFP-tagged version of the H134R mutant of Chlamydomonas reinhardtii channelrhodopsin 2 were created by standard laboratory procedures.
source: Self-inactivating lentiviral vector particles encoding an eYFP-tagged version of the H134R mutant of Chlamydomonas reinhardtii channelrhodopsin 2 (LVV-ChR2(H134R)), were created by standard laboratory procedures (Feola et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Feola et al., 2016.

claim: Lentiviral vector particles were used to transduce human atrial myocytes differentiated from a conditionally immortalised cell line.
source: Self-inactivating lentiviral vector particles encoding an eYFP-tagged version of the H134R mutant of Chlamydomonas reinhardtii channelrhodopsin 2 (LVV-ChR2(H134R)), were created by standard laboratory procedures (Feola et al., 2016) and used to transduce human atrial myocytes differentiated from a conditionally immortalised cell line (Harlaar et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure used.

claim: APs were recorded in single cells or small clusters of cells using the amphotericin-B perforated patch-clamp technique.
source: APs were recorded in single cells or small clusters of cells using the amphotericin-B perforated patch-clamp technique (Wilders, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wilders, 2006.

claim: Potentials were corrected for the calculated liquid junction potential.
source: Potentials were corrected for the calculated liquid junction potential (Barry and Lynch, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Barry and Lynch, 1991.
